stages.name: Emerging and developing economies
stages.title: Debt, capital flight and subsidy removal
stages.sub: How you can explain a developing country's debt problems and judge the market-orientated policy of cutting subsidies.

steps.q: A developing country's government spends more on roads and hospitals than it collects in tax, year after year. Where does the extra money come from?
steps.right: It borrows the money, often from abroad
steps.wrong: It simply prints more of its own currency each time
steps.hint: Think about who is willing to lend to a government that keeps spending more than it earns.

steps.right: A large amount owed to foreign lenders
steps.wrong: A large amount owed to its own citizens only
steps.hint: The borrowing in the last question came mostly from abroad. What has that left behind?

steps.q: Investors start to worry this country will struggle to repay its debts. What are foreign investors likely to do with money they already have invested there?
steps.right: Move it out of the country quickly
steps.wrong: Leave it invested and wait patiently
steps.hint: If you thought a country might default, would you want your savings sitting inside it?

steps.q: To free up money to repay its debts, the government has been keeping fuel prices low by paying part of the cost itself. What is this payment called?
steps.hint: The government is covering part of the price for consumers, not taxing anything.

steps.q: Facing this heavy debt burden, the government decides to stop paying the fuel subsidy and let the market set the price instead. What kind of strategy is scrapping the subsidy?
steps.right: A market-orientated strategy, letting prices adjust freely
steps.wrong: An interventionist strategy, controlling prices more closely
steps.hint: Is the government controlling the price more, or stepping back and letting supply and demand decide it?
steps.pre: Stopping this payment and letting the market set the price is

steps.q: Once the fuel subsidy is scrapped, the government no longer has to fund it. What does this free up for the government to spend on other things, and how might firms now compete on fuel prices?
steps.right: More funds are freed up, and firms compete more efficiently on price
steps.wrong: Fuel prices fall further and government spending stays the same
steps.hint: The money that used to go on the subsidy has to go somewhere else now, and firms are no longer protected from the true cost.

steps.q: Fuel prices jump sharply once the subsidy is gone. How are poorer households, who spend a large share of their income on fuel, likely to be affected?
steps.right: They are hit hardest, as fuel takes up more of their income
steps.wrong: They are barely affected, since everyone pays the same higher price
steps.hint: Think about whose budget is squeezed more by the same price rise.
